name: Aphids
symptoms: Curled, distorted, or yellowing leaves
Sticky honeydew coating on leaves and stems
Sooty mold growing on the honeydew
Stunted new growth and deformed buds
Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides
lifecycle: Egg — overwinters on host plant in cold climates
Nymph — 4 instars over 7-10 days to maturity
Adult — winged females disperse in summer; wingless females reproduce asexually (parthenogenesis)
10-30 generations per year depending on climate
One female can produce 80+ offspring without mating
treatmentOrganic: Spray strong jet of water to dislodge — repeat every 2 days
Apply insecticidal soap to infested foliage every 5-7 days
Release ladybugs, lacewings, or parasitic wasps
Spray neem oil weekly until populations crash
Dust diatomaceous earth on dry foliage as a barrier
treatmentChemical: Pyrethrin spray for fast knockdown
Imidacloprid systemic for severe ornamental infestations
Acetamiprid where bee-safety is required
Avoid neonicotinoids on flowering plants
prevention: Companion plant with marigolds, garlic, chives, and nasturtiums
Encourage beneficial insects with diverse flowering plants
Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen (lush growth attracts aphids)
Inspect new plants before introducing them
Use reflective mulch to confuse winged aphids

name: Armyworm
symptoms: Ragged holes chewed in leaves, often overnight
Skeletonised leaves with only veins remaining
Plants stripped down to the stalk in severe outbreaks
Frass (dark pellets) on leaves and at the plant base
Caterpillars feed at night and hide under debris by day
lifecycle: Egg — laid in clusters of 50-200 on leaves or grasses
Larva — 6 instars over 14-21 days; this is the damaging stage
Pupa — pupates in the soil for 7-14 days
Adult moth — lives 9-14 days and lays up to 1,500 eggs
3-6 generations per year, migrates over long distances
treatmentOrganic: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) at dusk every 5-7 days
Hand-pick larvae in the early morning or after dark
Apply spinosad spray for advanced infestations
Release Trichogramma egg parasitoid wasps
Apply nematode (Steinernema carpocapsae) drench to the soil
treatmentChemical: Chlorantraniliprole at first sign of damage
Lambda-cyhalothrin pyrethroid for emergency knockdown
Emamectin benzoate for resistant fall armyworm
Rotate insecticide classes to prevent resistance
prevention: Pheromone traps to monitor adult moth flights
Encourage natural enemies — birds, ground beetles, parasitic wasps
Maintain weed-free field borders that harbour egg-laying moths
Plant trap crops (e.g. napier grass border for maize)
Scout fields weekly during peak season
Till crop residue after harvest to expose pupae

name: Whitefly
symptoms: Tiny white moth-like insects fly up when foliage is disturbed
Yellowing, mottled, or curling leaves
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold growth
Stunted plants and reduced yields
Virus transmission (e.g. tomato yellow leaf curl, cassava mosaic)
lifecycle: Egg — laid on leaf undersides, hatches in 5-10 days
Nymph — 4 instars over 2-4 weeks, sessile after first instar
Pupa — non-feeding stage inside the final nymph skin
Adult — lives 30-60 days and lays 200-400 eggs
Continuous breeding in warm climates and greenhouses
treatmentOrganic: Hang yellow sticky traps near affected plants
Spray insecticidal soap on leaf undersides every 5-7 days
Apply neem oil at dusk every 7-10 days
Release Encarsia formosa parasitoid wasps in greenhouses
Vacuum adults from foliage in the early morning while sluggish
treatmentChemical: Pymetrozine for selective whitefly control
Pyriproxyfen insect growth regulator on nymphs
Acetamiprid systemic for ornamental crops
Spiromesifen for both nymphs and eggs
prevention: Use reflective silver mulch to repel adults
Install fine insect-mesh on greenhouse vents
Inspect transplants thoroughly before bringing them home
Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
Avoid planting whitefly-magnet hosts (e.g. poinsettia) near vegetables
Rotate to non-host crops in heavily infested fields

name: Thrips
symptoms: Silvery or bronze streaks on leaves and petals
Black specks of frass on damaged surfaces
Distorted growth and deformed flowers
Tomato spotted wilt virus transmission
Slender 1-2 mm insects visible with a hand lens
lifecycle: Egg — inserted into plant tissue, hatches in 3-5 days
Larva — 2 instars over 7-14 days on leaves and flowers
Pupa — pre-pupal and pupal stages in the soil or leaf litter
Adult — lives 30-45 days and lays 80+ eggs
Up to 15 generations per year in warm climates
treatmentOrganic: Hang blue sticky traps near affected plants
Spray spinosad every 7 days during outbreaks
Apply insecticidal soap to all leaf surfaces
Release predatory mites (Amblyseius cucumeris)
Drench soil with beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae)
treatmentChemical: Spinetoram for rotation with spinosad
Abamectin on persistent infestations
Methomyl for emergency knockdown (highly toxic — last resort)
Cyantraniliprole as a systemic option
prevention: Use insect-mesh screens on greenhouses (mesh < 0.2 mm)
Avoid planting near grassy field margins
Remove weeds that host thrips year-round
Mulch with reflective material to deter flight
Quarantine new ornamentals for 2 weeks before introducing

name: Spider Mites
symptoms: Fine speckling or stippling on upper leaf surfaces
Fine silken webbing on leaf undersides and between stems
Bronzed, dusty, or pale appearance on heavily infested leaves
Leaf drop and stunted growth in severe cases
Tiny (< 0.5 mm) red, yellow, or green mites visible with a hand lens
lifecycle: Egg — laid singly on leaf undersides, hatches in 3 days at 26 °C
Larva — 6-legged, feeds for 1-2 days
Protonymph + deutonymph — 8-legged immatures over 4-5 days
Adult — lives 2-4 weeks, female lays 100+ eggs
Complete life cycle in 5-20 days; many generations per season
treatmentOrganic: Spray strong jet of water on leaf undersides every 2-3 days
Apply insecticidal soap weekly to all foliage surfaces
Spray horticultural oil to smother eggs and adults
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
Increase humidity around houseplants — mites prefer dry conditions
treatmentChemical: Abamectin every 10-14 days
Bifenazate for resistant populations
Fenpyroximate IGR for outdoor crops
Avoid pyrethroids — they kill predatory mites worse than spider mites
prevention: Maintain adequate watering and humidity
Mist houseplant foliage regularly
Avoid dusty conditions that protect mites from predators
Inspect new plants under leaves for early webbing
Encourage native predators by reducing broad-spectrum spray use

name: Scale
symptoms: Small bumpy oval discs (1-5 mm) attached to stems and leaves
Yellow chlorotic spots beneath the scale insect
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on soft scale infestations
Branch dieback and overall plant decline
Heavily infested plants may shed leaves prematurely
lifecycle: Egg — laid under the female scale cover
Crawler — mobile newly-hatched stage; this is when scale is vulnerable
Settled nymph — inserts mouthparts and forms its protective covering
Adult female — lays 100-1000 eggs under her shell; legless and immobile
1-3 generations per year depending on species and climate
treatmentOrganic: Scrape scale off small infestations with a soft brush
Spray dormant horticultural oil on woody hosts in late winter
Apply summer-weight oil to active crawlers in spring/summer
Dab individual scales with rubbing alcohol on a cotton swab
Encourage parasitic wasps (Aphytis, Encarsia) and ladybirds
treatmentChemical: Imidacloprid soil drench for systemic ornamental control
Buprofezin IGR targeting crawlers
Pyriproxyfen on greenhouse infestations
Sulfoxaflor for tough soft-scale infestations
prevention: Inspect new plants for scale before bringing them home
Prune dense interior growth to expose hidden scales
Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen
Monitor with sticky tape wrapped around stems to catch crawlers
Maintain healthy plant vigor — stressed plants attract scale

name: Mealybugs
symptoms: White cottony or waxy masses on stems, leaf joints, and roots
Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on affected plants
Distorted new growth and dropping leaves
Heavy infestations cling to leaf undersides in cottony clusters
lifecycle: Egg — laid in cottony egg sacs, hatches in 7-10 days
Crawler — 1st instar nymphs disperse to feeding sites
Nymph — 3 instars over 6-10 weeks (longer for males)
Adult female — lives 2-3 months, lays 300-600 eggs
Males have wings and exist briefly to mate; do not feed
Continuous breeding indoors; 2-3 outdoor generations per year
treatmentOrganic: Dab individual mealybugs with 70 % isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab
Wash off colonies with strong water spray weekly
Apply insecticidal soap to all stem joints and undersides
Release Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (mealybug destroyer beetle)
Spray neem oil every 7 days to smother and disrupt growth
treatmentChemical: Acetamiprid for systemic control on ornamentals
Buprofezin growth regulator targeting nymphs
Spirotetramat for citrus mealybugs
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill mealybug predators
prevention: Quarantine new plants for 3-4 weeks before introducing
Wipe leaves regularly to detect early infestations
Avoid overcrowding plants — mealybugs spread by touch
Keep dust off leaves — encourages mealybugs and discourages predators
Repot houseplants in fresh sterile media every 1-2 years

name: Beetles
symptoms: Holes chewed in leaves, sometimes skeletonising the leaf
Damaged flowers and developing fruit
Visible adult beetles feeding in groups
Larvae (grubs) damaging roots in the soil
Wilting plants where root feeding is heavy
lifecycle: Egg — laid in soil or on host foliage
Larva (grub) — 3 instars over weeks to months, feeds on roots
Pupa — pupates in soil chamber for 2-3 weeks
Adult — flies, feeds, and mates for several weeks
1 generation per year for most species (e.g. Japanese beetle, cucumber beetle)
treatmentOrganic: Hand-pick adults in the early morning and drown in soapy water
Apply neem oil weekly to deter feeding and disrupt eggs
Spray pyrethrin or spinosad for active infestations
Apply beneficial nematodes (Heterorhabditis) to soil for grubs
Use floating row covers until flowering for cucurbits
treatmentChemical: Carbaryl as a broad-spectrum knockdown on adults
Imidacloprid soil drench for grubs
Chlorantraniliprole on larval populations
Rotate to avoid resistance
prevention: Companion plant with garlic, chives, and tansy
Use kaolin clay foliar coating to deter feeding
Hand-tilling exposes pupae to birds and weather
Avoid drought-stressing plants — stressed plants attract beetles
Maintain healthy lawn to reduce grub habitat
Use pheromone traps only at field perimeters (they can attract more beetles)

name: Caterpillars
symptoms: Large irregular holes chewed in leaves, often from leaf margins inward
Skeletonised foliage where only the leaf veins remain
Dark green or black frass pellets on leaves and at the plant base
Silken threads or rolled leaves sheltering young larvae
Tunnelling damage in heads of cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower
Visible larvae feeding on undersides of leaves at dawn and dusk
lifecycle: Egg — laid singly or in small clusters on leaf undersides, hatches in 3-10 days
Larva — 5 instars over 14-30 days; this is the foliage-damaging stage
Pupa — chrysalis or cocoon attached to stems, leaves, or soil for 7-14 days
Adult moth or butterfly — lives 1-3 weeks and lays 100-600 eggs
2-5 generations per year in temperate zones; year-round in tropics
treatmentOrganic: Hand-pick larvae morning and evening on small plantings
Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) at dusk every 5-7 days
Apply spinosad spray for larger or more advanced infestations
Release Trichogramma egg parasitoid wasps before populations peak
Cover susceptible crops with fine insect mesh during peak moth flights
treatmentChemical: Chlorantraniliprole for selective lepidopteran control
Indoxacarb on resistant populations
Emamectin benzoate for severe outbreaks
Rotate insecticide modes of action to slow resistance build-up
prevention: Hang pheromone traps to monitor adult moth flights and time sprays
Encourage parasitic wasps, predatory bugs, and insectivorous birds
Use floating row covers from transplant until harvest on brassicas
Remove weedy hosts from field margins between seasons
Inspect leaf undersides weekly for egg clusters and crush by hand
Rotate brassica plantings to break the lifecycle

name: Leaf Miners
symptoms: Pale serpentine tunnels (mines) winding through the leaf tissue
Translucent blotches or blister-like patches on affected leaves
Tiny black frass dots visible inside the mines when held up to the light
Premature leaf yellowing and drop on heavily mined foliage
Reduced yields on leafy crops such as spinach, chard, and lettuce
Small adult flies (1-2 mm) resting on upper leaf surfaces
lifecycle: Egg — adult female punctures leaf and inserts eggs into the tissue, hatches in 2-5 days
Larva — 3 instars feed inside the leaf for 5-10 days, creating the mine
Pupa — mature larva drops to the soil or pupates inside the mine for 7-14 days
Adult — lives 15-30 days; female creates many feeding/oviposition punctures
Continuous overlapping generations in warm climates and greenhouses
treatmentOrganic: Pinch out and destroy mined leaves as soon as they appear
Hang yellow sticky traps to catch egg-laying adults
Spray neem oil weekly to deter oviposition and disrupt larvae
Release Diglyphus isaea parasitoid wasps in greenhouse crops
Apply spinosad at first sign of mines to kill larvae through the leaf surface
treatmentChemical: Abamectin for translaminar control of larvae inside leaves
Cyromazine insect growth regulator on persistent infestations
Pyrethrins for fast knockdown of adult flies
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that destroy parasitoid populations
prevention: Use fine insect mesh (less than 0.5 mm) on greenhouse vents and tunnels
Rotate crops to break the local lifecycle
Remove weedy hosts such as lambsquarters and chickweed
Plough or solarise soil after harvest to kill overwintering pupae
Plant trap crops such as columbine or velvet beans at field margins
Inspect transplants thoroughly before introducing them

name: Fruit Flies
symptoms: Small puncture marks (stings) on developing fruit surface
Soft brown spots or premature yellowing around the sting site
Maggots tunnelling inside the flesh of ripening fruit
Fruit drop before maturity, often with oozing exudate
Secondary rot and fermenting smell from infested fruit
Adult flies (5-8 mm) with banded wings hovering near ripening crops
lifecycle: Egg — laid in batches of 2-15 beneath the fruit skin, hatches in 1-3 days
Larva — 3 instars feed inside the fruit for 6-14 days
Pupa — mature larva exits the fruit, pupates in the soil for 7-14 days
Adult — lives 30-60 days, female lays 800-1000 eggs over her lifetime
8-10 overlapping generations per year in subtropical and tropical zones
treatmentOrganic: Hang protein bait traps (hydrolysed yeast or commercial lure) at 1 per 10 trees
Bag developing fruit with paper or fine mesh sleeves before colour change
Collect and destroy all fallen and stung fruit daily during the season
Apply spinosad-based GF-120 bait sprays in droplets on host foliage
Release Diachasmimorpha parasitoid wasps where commercially available
treatmentChemical: Malathion bait sprays combined with protein hydrolysate
Lambda-cyhalothrin cover sprays on emergency outbreaks
Methyl eugenol male annihilation blocks for Bactrocera dorsalis
Cue-lure traps for melon and cucurbit fly species
prevention: Practise strict field sanitation — remove all fallen fruit weekly
Solarise or deep-bury culled fruit to kill larvae and pupae
Cultivate soil under trees during pupation to expose pupae to predators
Harvest fruit slightly under-ripe in high-pressure areas
Establish area-wide management with neighbours on shared trap networks
Plant early-maturing varieties to escape peak fly populations

name: Snails and Slugs
symptoms: Irregular ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in leaves and stems
Shiny silvery mucous trails on foliage, soil, and pots
Seedlings sheared off at the soil line overnight
Damaged ripe strawberries, lettuce hearts, and tender hostas
Concentrated feeding damage on basal leaves close to the ground
Active feeding at night, after rain, and in early morning
lifecycle: Egg — laid in clusters of 20-100 in damp soil crevices, hatches in 10-30 days
Juvenile — miniature versions of adults, mature over 3-6 months
Adult — slugs live 1-2 years; some snails live up to 5 years
Hermaphrodites — each individual can lay eggs after mating
Multiple egg-laying events per year under moist conditions
treatmentOrganic: Apply iron-phosphate bait pellets around susceptible plantings
Hand-pick at night by torchlight or trap under wet boards by day
Set shallow beer traps sunk to ground level near affected plants
Ring beds with copper tape or copper-mesh barriers
Encourage natural predators — ground beetles, hedgehogs, ducks, and frogs
treatmentChemical: Metaldehyde pellets in fenced bait stations away from pets and wildlife
Methiocarb pellets on commercial-scale infestations
Avoid scattering bait on bare soil where it leaches with rain
Always follow label rates — over-use harms beneficial fauna
prevention: Water in the morning so the soil surface dries before nightfall
Remove ground-level hiding places — boards, rocks, leaf litter, mulch piles
Use rough mulches (crushed eggshells, sharp grit, wood ash) as barriers
Cultivate soil in early spring to expose overwintering eggs
Plant slug-resistant varieties (e.g. red lettuce, rosemary, lavender)
Keep grass strips short to reduce daytime shelter

name: Root-Knot Nematodes
symptoms: Knobbly galls and swellings along the roots of affected plants
Stunted growth despite adequate water and fertiliser
Yellowing of older leaves and mid-day wilting in warm weather
Reduced yields and small misshapen tubers or root crops
Patchy crop failure in fields, often worsening year on year
Microscopic worms (less than 1 mm) visible inside galls under a hand lens
lifecycle: Egg — laid in gelatinous masses on root surfaces, 200-500 per female
Juvenile (J1, J2) — second-stage juveniles hatch and seek host roots
Sedentary feeding stage (J3, J4) — embedded in root tissue, triggers gall formation
Adult female — pear-shaped, remains inside the root and produces eggs
Complete lifecycle in 25-30 days at 27 degrees C; multiple generations per season
treatmentOrganic: Plant Tagetes patula (French marigold) as a biofumigant before susceptible crops
Incorporate brassica residues or mustard cover crops then turn under
Drench soil with Purpureocillium lilacinum or Pochonia chlamydosporia bioagents
Add high rates of compost to boost antagonistic soil microbiota
Solarise soil under clear plastic for 4-6 weeks at peak summer temperatures
treatmentChemical: Fluensulfone applied pre-plant on heavily infested fields
Fluopyram seed treatments on commercial vegetable crops
Oxamyl drench on protected high-value crops (highly toxic — last resort)
Always observe pre-harvest intervals and worker re-entry periods
prevention: Rotate susceptible crops with non-host cereals or grasses for 2-3 seasons
Plant resistant cultivars (look for the Mi gene on tomato seed packets)
Quarantine new transplants and inspect root systems before planting
Sterilise tools and boots between fields to prevent soil movement
Maintain high soil organic matter to support antagonistic microbes
Avoid moving soil from infested fields to clean ones

name: Weevils
symptoms: Notched leaf margins from adult feeding (classic C-shaped scallops)
Wilting and collapse of shoots tunnelled by larvae
Round exit holes on stored grains, beans, and tubers
Larvae visible inside seeds, stems, or below the soil on roots
Frass packed inside tunnels and chambers within stems or seeds
Adults with distinctive elongated snouts (1-15 mm) on foliage and stored produce
lifecycle: Egg — laid in soil, on plant tissue, or chewed into seeds and stems
Larva — legless C-shaped grub feeds inside plant tissue for 2-8 weeks
Pupa — pupates within the feeding chamber or in soil for 1-3 weeks
Adult — lives 6-12 months; many species do not fly and disperse by walking
1-3 generations per year for field species; continuous in stored grain
treatmentOrganic: Apply sticky bands around tree trunks to trap flightless adults
Drench soil with entomopathogenic nematodes (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora)
Hand-collect adults at night by shaking foliage onto a white sheet
Apply diatomaceous earth to stored grain to abrade adult cuticles
Spray neem oil to deter oviposition on susceptible crops
treatmentChemical: Pirimiphos-methyl on stored grain to control granary and rice weevils
Bifenthrin perimeter sprays for vine and root weevil adults
Imidacloprid drenches on ornamentals heavily attacked by root weevil larvae
Phosphine fumigation of sealed grain stores (licensed operators only)
prevention: Store grain and pulses in airtight, well-dried containers below 14 percent moisture
Freeze suspect seed for 72 hours at -18 degrees C before storage
Rotate field crops to break host continuity for specialist weevils
Maintain weed-free margins where adults shelter and overwinter
Inspect bulbs, tubers, and seed lots carefully before planting
Encourage ground beetles, shrews, and birds as natural predators

name: Grasshoppers
symptoms: Large ragged bites taken from leaf margins and whole leaves stripped
Heavy defoliation of cereals, vegetables, and pasture in dry seasons
Damage concentrated at field edges adjacent to grasslands and fallows
Cut stems and shredded seed heads in maize, sorghum, and millet
Visible nymphs and adults hopping or flying when disturbed
Frass pellets on the ground beneath roosting sites
lifecycle: Egg — pods of 20-100 eggs laid in soil in late summer, overwinter in place
Nymph — 5-6 instars over 30-50 days; wingless hoppers congregate in bands
Adult — fully winged, lives 60-90 days, disperses widely in search of food
Female lays 7-30 egg pods over her adult life
Usually 1 generation per year; some tropical species multivoltine
treatmentOrganic: Apply Nosema locustae protozoan bait early on young nymphs
Spray Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium acridum biopesticides at first hatch
Release or attract chickens, ducks, guinea fowl, and wild birds
Cultivate egg-laying sites in autumn to expose pods to weather and predators
Drag a metal pole or rope across grass margins to dislodge and crush nymphs
treatmentChemical: Carbaryl bait blocks scattered on field edges during hopper bands
Fipronil ultra-low-volume sprays for swarm and outbreak control
Lambda-cyhalothrin perimeter sprays on emergency defoliation
Coordinate area-wide treatments with regional plant protection services
prevention: Plant grass border trap crops (e.g. napier or sudangrass) at field edges
Maintain habitat for predators — kestrels, shrikes, ground beetles, spiders
Disc or harrow known egg-laying ground in autumn or early spring
Avoid leaving large fallow blocks adjacent to high-value crops
Scout field edges weekly from emergence through to adult flight
Use early-maturing crop varieties to escape peak hopper damage
